## Executive Summary
Waselnuk (developer relations, Unblocked) argues the binding constraint on agentic coding is no longer model intelligence but *context*: a fresh agent session is intelligent but knows nothing about how a particular organization ships software, and that gap compounds as a team moves from tab completion to single agents to parallel agents to background agents — turning into correction loops ("wasted search tokens"), rework time, and a review tax on AI code reviewers. He names two local maxima that stall: the curated-context trap (hand-written markdown describing a project, which then has to be distributed, rots like every other doc, and needs someone with the "taste" to maintain it for everyone) and the MCP plateau (an agent may never call the server at all depending on the tool description, or it stops at the first plausible hit because of *satisfaction-of-search bias* — "access to information is not understanding"). He then gives six properties a real context engine owes you, reports an A/B where the same prompt on the same model burned 21M tokens without the engine and 10.8M with it and finished about two hours sooner, and releases three open-source tools, including a workshop that builds a *relational* context engine and teaches the agent to discover a schema and write deterministic queries against it — because RAG alone cannot answer "what are the open PRs I worked on in the last week with authentication?"

- **Context cost compounds with agent autonomy.** Tab completion is cheap to get wrong (a human's own "context engine" rejects the bad suggestion in their head); unattended and parallel agents have no such rejector, so a bad-context run produces correction loops and wasted search tokens, and "that is not acceptable with the tokenomics we have coming."

# 6-dim Harness w/ MEMORY via Textual Gradients

## Executive Summary
The video walks through MemoHarness ("Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience", arXiv:2607.14159, Huang et al., University of Notre Dame / LMU Munich / USC, published July 14, 2026), a method for treating the agent harness — the control layer around a frozen LLM — as a learnable object via "nonparametric meta-learning." The harness is decomposed into six separable dimensions (context assembly, tool interaction, generation controls, workflow topology, memory management, output processing), and a controller LLM learns per-dimension corrections from its own execution history using "textual gradients": failures are diagnosed against the reasoning trace and attributed to a specific dimension rather than logged as a generic task failure. At test time the system retrieves similar past cases (successes, anti-patterns, distilled rules) by embedding similarity and the controller edits a case-specific harness for each incoming task. Reported gains: Terminal Bench 72→80% (GPT-5.3 Codex), 50→73% (GLM5), 33→44% (DeepSeek v3), and a finance-agent curve rising 42→65% before plateauing. The presenter is enthusiastic about the background-learning property but explicitly flags two shaky assumptions: that the controller LLM is near-"almighty" at architecture design, and that English-textual gradients are a sufficient substitute for real optimization.

## Key Points
- The core argument: a single fixed global harness is "fundamentally mismatched" because it is optimized for average performance and can be systematically wrong for identifiable task subclasses — e.g. narrowly-specified code generation wants one-shot tool calls, no retrieval, no persistent memory, strict output extraction, while long-horizon repo repair wants repo inspection, multiple tool calls, persistent state analysis, and separate planning/execution phases.
- Harness design is framed as "conditional computation itself": like a mixture-of-experts model activating different experts per token, an adaptive agent should activate different external computational structures per task.
- MemoHarness is nonparametric — no tensor weights of the core LLM are modified. It is meta-learning over the control layer only: how context is assembled, which tools are allowed, how memory is kept across steps, and how output is parsed.

# From LOOPS to GRAPHS: AI Agents Learn Graph-Based Error Corrections

## Executive Summary
A walkthrough of the paper *Experience Memory Graph: One-Shot Error Correction for Agents* (UESTC Chengdu, arXiv:2607.13884, published 2026-07-15). Its core move is to stop asking a failed agent to *verbally* reflect on why it failed, and instead represent the failed trajectory and a successful expert trajectory as directed action-decision graphs, then compute the structural difference between them with a deterministic optimal-transport algorithm — fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) matching — and store the resulting edit operators (delete / insert / relabel) as reusable corrections. All the graph mathematics happens offline at training time; at test time the agent does no graph math at all, it embeds the task description and retrieves the pre-computed natural-language corrections from a vector store via 20-nearest-neighbour cosine similarity, so a small local model gets the benefit of reflection it is not smart enough to perform. The presenter rates the training-time half as "a beautiful solution" and the test-time half as its weak point — "we are back to the RAG system from 5 years ago".

## Key Points
- The status quo ("you failed, reflect on why, try again") has two named flaws: it is **expensive** (the LLM runs several times per test case, "millions of tokens, no result") and it **depends on the model being smart enough to diagnose its own hallucination** — small 4B/8B local models are not, and "get stuck in infinite error loops".
- The replacement is a shift from natural-language guesswork to a **deterministic mathematical graph-matching algorithm**. Graphs: nodes = actions, edges = observation-conditioned transitions. Real graphs are large — "sometimes 10,000 nodes or up to millions of nodes".
- The matcher is **fused Gromov-Wasserstein**, i.e. a node/content cost *fused* with a pairwise relational structure cost, minimised by iteratively shuffling nodes until an optimal **soft assignment matrix** ("transport plan", a heat map) is found: rows are nodes of the failed graph G, columns nodes of the expert graph G′, a bright cell (i,k) means node i corresponds to node k.
- The **Wasserstein** term maps semantically identical actions together; the **Gromov** term is what stops "take the apple" at step 2 being matched to "take the apple" at step 50 under a different environment, because the structural penalty would be too high. It compares relations *within* each graph rather than requiring both graphs in a shared coordinate system, so it works on **non-isomorphic** graphs.
